audit.recode_to: kind: unchanged (weight-hedged, QS-HEDGED; heavy = CV: and CVV, CV: outranks CVV). edge: 'unbounded' -> 'right' with a four-mora right-edge window in prule (catalog convention as in mana1295/nepa1254): 'main stress may not fall more than four morae (vowels) from the end of the word; inside that window stress the first long vowel, else the first diphthong (for some speakers any non-final diphthong), else the first syllable of the window' (Biggs 1969:132-3 rules 1-3,5 as quoted verbatim in Schutz 1985:9; Biggs 1978:700 'among the final four, which is as far forward as phrase-stress may move'; Harlow 2007:82 and Bauer 1993:546-7 as relayed by Culhane 2024:1070 and Thompson et al. 2011:1983; Mixdorff et al. 2018:631; Keegan 2023). Biggs' own examples show the window overriding 'leftmost long vowel' in words >4 morae: aanIwaniwa, kaarAmuramu, PaarEmoremo, haaEreere carry heaviest stress on the fourth vowel from the end, not on the initial long vowel (Biggs 1969:133 rule 4, in Schutz 1985:9). quote/cite: replace the StressTyp2-carried Hyman 1977:51 tail with its primary, Hohepa 1967:10, verbatim in Schutz 1985:8: 'stem stress is predictable... Major stress will fall on the first syllable containing a geminate cluster, if none, then on the first syllable with a non-identical vowel cluster, and if none, then on the first syllable. Secondary stress will fall on the subsequent syllable which fills the highest order of precedence after the major stress...'. domain/hedge note: Biggs 1978:699 'the fact that single words said alone are final phrases, and stressed accordingly, has given rise to the belief that Maori has word-initial stress. However, in non-final phrases any appropriately-placed word takes phrase-stress on the penultimate syllable'; Schutz 1985:22-23 'Accent in Maori cannot be described as either phonemic or predictable'; keep QS-HEDGED.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every de Lacy 2003 handout item quoted in the record ((19)-(21), (24)-(25)) is verbatim in the held txt at lines 137-188 (handout pp.3-4), and both Keegan 2024 passages (pp.59, 66) are verbatim in the held Te Reo 66 file; only the Hyman 1977:51 tail is database-carried with no held primary, which the record already flags. (2) The deciding source is a 2003 OT conference handout whose stress rule is background, not description; I fetched sources its published siblings (de Lacy 2002 MITWPL 44, author copy p.4; de Lacy 2004 Blackwell reader p.498), which repeat 'stress falls on a bimoraic syllable, otherwise the initial', add trochaic left-aligned feet and one-PrWd-per-bimoraic-morpheme, and add a dialect note (some dialects do not stress word-final diphthongs) -- all consistent with our weight-sensitive, unbounded-leftmost-heavy, CVV-heavy, no-root-internal-secondary coding. sources.quote: 'Bimoraic syllables contain either a long vowel or a diphthong. For present purposes, it is enough to say that stress falls on a bimoraic syllable, otherwise the initial. (5) [tama] boy, [taNata] man, [marae] meeting area, [kuri:] dog ... Maori employs trochaic feet and aims to have them at the left edge of the PrWd if possible. Every bimoraic root or affix is contained inside its own PrWd.'
